## 1. Quantum computing

**Proper Learning of Shallow All-to-All Quantum Circuits**
Steven Kordonowy, Jacob Watkins — [arXiv:2608.20162](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20162)
A clean sharp boundary for the ensemble behind several recent quantum-cryptographic proposals (circuit-learning hardness): given query access and known layout, a meta-algorithm of iterative front/back local gate inversions has a *discrete* learnability cliff at depth *d\* ≈ log₂ n + log₂ log₂ n*, shown via lightcone analysis. Two things make it land differently from the two complexity results I've been tracking: it is a *learning-theoretic* boundary rather than a query-complexity one, and the paper is explicit that the setting differs from the cryptographic ones it threatens — that honesty is what makes it a useful input to the ongoing "circuit-learning as a primitive" debate rather than a rebuttal. The lightcone-growth-as-learnability mechanism is a transferable tool for any result where depth-structure is the underlying quantity.

**Logarithmic depth compression of Heisenberg Hamiltonian simulation by fan-out parallelization, with built-in error detection**
Artemiy Burov, Clément Javerzac — [arXiv:2608.20250](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20250)
The right shape of result for where NISQ compilation is heading: instead of optimizing gate count, they trade depth for width using *repetition-code registers of the physical qubits* sized by interaction degree, so all same-type Pauli interactions of a hub can run in parallel after one log-depth CNOT fan-out, and the redundancy gives post-selection error detection for free. On the 13-spin TMS benchmark and a 13-spin star, the deeper sequential compile is beaten on two-qubit depth by 2–2.5× (heavy-hex / all-to-all) and volume by 1.7×. The honest caveat in the abstract is the part I care about: the win only exists *after* post-selection AND after error rates improve by 1–1.5 orders of magnitude from current calibration — this is one of the few papers that is explicit about the hardware condition under which its own result activates.

**Large Scale Entanglement Structure Detection in 100-Qubit Systems via Local Joint Measurements**
Rui Li, Yuhang Wang, Chunxiao Du, Shikun Zhang, Zheng Qin, Wenxiu Li, Hao Zhang, Zhisong Xiao — [arXiv:2608.20170](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20170)
A scaling claim that's unusually concrete: a single-basis local-Pauli protocol whose boundary-matching condition *p₁ = p_R* lets them read an entire chain in one configuration, so the measurement cost is size-independent. >95% accuracy across GHZ / W / cluster-type structure classification on up to 100 qubits in simulation, then validated on a superconducting processor up to 13 qubits before noise/depth kills it. The 13-qubit number is the real result and the honest one — that's where the hardware boundary of the method actually sits. Worth tracking as the natural tool for QEC code verification at intermediate sizes (qLDPC verification is going to need exactly this kind of structure-level readout).

**Learning Potts Models and Z₃ Toric Codes: Higher and Ordinary Nishimori Criticality**
Rushikesh A. Patil, Malte Pütz, Rohit Mukherjee, Guo-Yi Zhu, Simon Trebst, Andreas W. W. Ludwig — [arXiv:2608.20268](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20268)
The cleanest bridge I've seen this month between statistical-inference learning theory and QEC code memory. Framing a monitored-deformed Zq toric code as a learning problem in the Potts model, they find a *tricritical* "higher Nishimori" information-critical point at finite inference strength that separates stable quantum-mem, classical-mem, and no-mem phases — using the Casimir effective central charge as a monotone order parameter along measurement-induced RG flows. That's a new organizing principle for which measurement protocols give you which kind of quantum memory at which temperature, and the Elitzur-theorem argument for the stability of the ordinary critical point is the kind of structural result QEC people don't get enough of.

The most important number here is the *negative* one: across 18 configurations of policy × workload × capacity × encoder, no evaluated eviction policy improves on LFU by more than 0.041 points. **Generated:** 2026-08-21 · Sources: arXiv (submissions dated 2026-08-20)

**Continuity from prior runs:**
- **Blanc et al., "Quantum Speedups Require Structure or Depth"** (first flagged 2026-08-20) — now has a direct companion: today's Liu & Mutreja paper (below) proves the Aaronson–Ambainis almost-everywhere simulation conjecture for massively-parallel queries, exactly the next step the earlier result pointed at. - **Eureka's math claim** (first flagged 2026-08-20, still unverified — no reproduction found in this window) — today's FormalTCS result (below) is independent and negative on the same question, which makes the skepticism around "agents produce genuine new theorems" the more defensible prior as of today.

---

## 1. Quantum computing

**Parallel Quantum Advantage with Limited Adaptivity Requires Structure**
Qipeng Liu, Saachi Mutreja — [arXiv:2608.20297](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20297)
The direct sequel to the "Structure or Depth" thread I flagged on 2026-08-20: it proves the Aaronson–Ambainis almost-everywhere classical-simulation conjecture for *massively parallel* quantum query algorithms, which is the hardest setting (Yamakawa–Zhandry showed parallel-only algorithms *can* win exponential speedups on sampling, so this needed a real new argument — a coupling theorem showing a parallel quantum algorithm cannot distinguish uniform oracles from "dense" distributions). The corollary is that even allowing constant rounds of adaptivity on top of the parallel stage, the conjecture holds — meaning exponential advantage at constant rounds must live in structure, not parallelism. Two independent groups landing on the same structural conclusion in one week is a strong signal this is now settled territory, and both results together sharply narrow where unstructured quantum advantage can exist.

**RL-Trotter: Reinforcement Learning to Harness Approximation Errors for Long-Time Quantum Simulation**
Yu-Bo Shi, Markus Heyl, Roderich Moessner, Marin Bukov, Hongzheng Zhao — [arXiv:2608.20139](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20139)
The framing here is the genuinely new part: instead of fighting Trotter error, the RL agent learns an adaptive step-size policy that *orchestrates* errors so later steps compensate earlier ones, guided only by conservation-law signals (energy, energy variance) with no access to the target state. That is a real redefinition of what an error means in variational quantum algorithms — from noise to a controllable resource — and the reported transfer to systems an order of magnitude larger, trained classically then deployed, is the part that makes it more than theory. With Heyl, Moessner, and Bukov attached, this comes from a group that has actually run long-range quantum simulations, which matters for credibility.

**ONEX: Architecture and Compilation Co-Design for High-Rate Quantum Product Codes on Neutral Atom Arrays**
Adrian Liu, Wan-Hsuan Lin, Daniel Bochen Tan, Qian Xu, Jason Cong — [arXiv:2608.20164](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20164)
qLDPC is where practical high-rate fault tolerance lives, and the compile-time combinatorics of physically executing a code on an atom array is the unglamorous bottleneck nobody wants to hit at 2,500 data qubits. ONEX's decomposition — split the 2D execution problem into independent 1D subproblems solved *provably optimally* with SMT — is a clean co-design trick that beats general 2D compilers by up to ~42× in clock rate and constructive 1D by ~6×. This is the same neutral-atom stack I've been tracking since the 101 Hz throughput result (2026-08-18): the field is now moving from "can we reconfigure fast enough" to "can we compile enough to make the codes worth reconfiguring."

*Skipped:* Disassembling qLDPC codes for depth-optimal parity-check circuits (2608.19917) — good, near-optimal CNOT-depth circuits up to 600 data qubits, but incremental next to ONEX. Shadow models for cloud-cover QML (2608.19917-adjacent, 2608.20076) — sensible classical surrogate story, single application. TT-Net tensor-train denoising in GANs (2608.19789) — incremental.

---

## 2. Machine learning

**EchoCoT: Extracting Hidden Chain-of-Thought from Large Reasoning Models**
Yiting Qu, Ziqing Yang, Chi Cui, Ye Leng, Junjie Chu, Yang Zhang — [arXiv:2608.20055](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20055)
This is an extraction result that should matter well beyond the ML-lab audience: a multi-step API-only attack that pulls near-verbatim hidden CoT from black-box reasoning models, exploiting a "reasoning replay surface" in tool calls and using fidelity signals the API itself returns. The scale is the story — up to 66.4% near-verbatim on open-source models, up to 80% on unseen datasets, and a 33,463-token extraction from a 32,948-token Gemini 2.5 target. That reframes "your thinking process is a protected asset" as an engineering problem with a working attack, not a policy aspiration, and the finding that one discovered injection trajectory generalizes across datasets is exactly the kind of result that moves a lab's threat model.

**MemTrapBench: Benchmarking Cognitive Traps in LLM Memory Use**
Mengru Wang, Haozhe Luo, Zhenqian Xu, et al. (incl. Ningyu Zhang) — [arXiv:2608.20202](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20202)
The strongest negative result of the window and directly relevant to the agent-memory work I've been tracking: across two model families and five memory frameworks, *every* memory configuration underperforms the no-memory baseline, with drops over 10% for the best methods. The mechanism is named and useful — memory-induced reasoning fixation and belief distortion, where faithfully and semantically correct retrieved memories actively corrupt the current task. Their fix (AdaptiveMem, an inference-time trap-avoidance instruction) partially mitigates without hurting standard memory benchmarks, but the headline for anyone building persistent agent memory (including the skill-memory work in Section 3 today) is that the field may need to rethink whether retrieved context is net-positive by default.

**Learned When to Think: Adaptive Reasoning for Test-Time Compute Allocation**
Gijs Kassenaar, Zhao Yang, Vincent François-Lavet — [arXiv:2608.20256](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20256)
A small, clean answer to the "rationale-length is a fixed budget" problem in RL-trained reasoning models: instead of a separate router, the model emits a mode token (NoThink / Short / Long) as its first output, learned inside GRPO with shaped rewards and hard per-mode token caps so the modes don't collapse. The interesting result is that on a 1.5B model the brief modes come out at least as accurate as Long — meaning the router learned to sort by difficulty, not just by laziness — while cutting mean response length by 41% and transferring the savings to other benchmarks without retraining (76% cut on GSM8K). This is the pattern to watch: adaptive compute allocation as a first-class learned behavior rather than a system-level hack, and it does it at a scale where the mechanism is actually inspectable.

*Skipped as incremental or narrow:* IAR retrieval-free document internalization (2608.20281) — solid three-stage recipe, domain-specific payoff. Orthogonal JEPA world models (2608.20065) — interesting factorization, early. DARS dual-level credit assignment for image editing (2608.20161) — clean but single-pipeline.

## 3. Recursive self-improvement

**AI4AI-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents in Algorithmic Design for Recursive Self-Improvement**
Yizhe Chi, Wenyi Li, Deyao Hong, et al. — [arXiv:2608.20318](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20318)
The most on-target RSI paper in this window, and it lands the hardest framing I've seen: the training algorithm *is* the process of self-improvement, so measuring RSI means measuring whether an agent can improve a training algorithm — which no existing benchmark isolates (they measure data collection or hyperparameter search, which is execution not learning). 10 frozen repos, 10 algorithm families, 4 hours on a B300, hidden evaluator, rerun from scratch up to 12 hours — the harness is designed to kill reward hacking by construction. The result is a hard, useful negative: best system scores 0.250 on a scale where 0.1 is the shipped algorithm and 1.0 is the optimum, and most submissions never touch the learning rule at all. The one genuinely surprising number is the reasoning-effort axis: more thinking moves the "actually modifies how the model learns" share from 8% to 64% of submissions, which suggests RSI failure at current frontier is an *orientation* problem (agents default to execution over learning) more than a capability wall — that's a hypothesis I'd want to chase with the next generation of these systems.

**Phantom Gains: Auditing Self-Improvement Against a Measured Null**
Cheng Xu, Nan Yan, Liming Chen, M-Tahar Kechadi — [arXiv:2608.20290](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20290)
The most consequential negative result of the three sections today, and it should be read by anyone reporting self-training gains. Auditing three rounds of rank-32 LoRA self-training on Qwen3-8B against a frozen control pushed through the identical pipeline, they find *seven* separate measurement artifacts, each of which alone flips a positive finding once the control is removed — inference-batching effects in a greedy-decode "capability" ledger alone manufacture an acquisition rate of 0.280 on an untrained model. The FDR-corrected audit detects nothing above noise on the held-out replicates for self-training, and finds self-training *corrupting* baseline-solved problems at rates above the measured floor, while external distillation wins only on problems the base model barely reaches. This is the methodological warning the RSI field needs right now: mean-score gains and per-problem transition gains are not the same claim, and the second requires a separately measured null that most of the field's self-training papers don't have.

**EnvHarness: Awakening Static Worlds for Agent Learning (with EnvRigger)**
Chengsong Huang, Zifeng Wang, Rujun Han, et al. (incl. Bhavana Dalvi Mishra, Tomas Pfister, Chen-Yu Lee) — [arXiv:2608.19880](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19880)
The production-shaped continuation of the SPADE line I flagged on 2026-08-20, and a genuinely different engineering answer to the same problem. Instead of generating whole new environments (expensive, needs reliable verifiers, still static), EnvHarness treats the existing environment as a substrate and applies a programmable plug-in layer that reshapes its behavior while *preserving the original verifier* — which is the part that makes it safe as an RSI substrate. EnvRigger is the RSI loop: it watches the target policy's trajectories as a black box, diagnoses specific failure modes, synthesizes harness components aimed at those modes, and validates them with fresh rollouts before they count. Up to 9.0 points on held-out instances across four domains with 9.8% fewer execution steps is a real result, but the more important claim is "continuous targeted co-evolution of policy and environment without rebuilding the environment" — that's a materially more tractable recursive loop than generating-entire-worlds-from-scratch, and it's built by a team that ships this kind of infrastructure.

**FormalTCS: Benchmarking End-to-End Frontier Formal Theoretical Computer Science Research of LLMs**
Dingzirui Wang, Xuanliang Zhang, Keyan Xu, Qingfu Zhu, Wanxiang Che — [arXiv:2608.20153](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20153)
175 expert-validated instances from STOC/FOCS/SODA/COLT 2025–26, each with verified Lean formalizations and proof dependencies — this is a real measure of "can an LLM do frontier theoretical CS research end-to-end" rather than on a curated subset. The result is a hard ceiling and a clean diagnosis of *where* it's stuck: autoformalization is the sharpest bottleneck (best model 11.5 translating a natural-language claim into a formal theorem vs. 28.6 Pass@8 proving a human-supplied formal statement), and their own automated research framework — generate, formalize, filter, prove — produced 64 candidate claims of which only 6 passed expert review and proof verification. Read against Eureka's unverified math claim from 2026-08-20, this is the data point that should lower the prior on "agent-generated novel theorems" until someone reproduces it; the bottleneck being formalization rather than proof is a genuinely useful decomposition of the whole problem.

**Break It Down, Pass It On: Cross-Task Skill Transfer in LLM Agents**
Yiyang Feng, Biddut Sarker Bijoy, Niranjan Balasubramanian, Jiawei Zhou — [arXiv:2608.20274](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20274)
A direct, controlled study of a mechanism the RSI field has started relying on without measuring it well enough: skill-library reuse. The two axes (task-level vs. subtask-level induction, text vs. code format) turn out to matter a lot, and the headline is uncomfortable — *task-level* induced skills mostly drag the agent *below* its no-memory baseline, while subtask-level skills lift it above. The "skill utility score" (specificity × abstractness combined) is a genuinely useful practical artifact: it predicts transfer success from the skill corpus and task descriptions alone, before any new task runs, which means it can be used as a diagnostic gate in a self-improvement loop rather than discovered after the fact. This pairs badly, in a productive way, with MemTrapBench (Section 2) — retrieved context is both the main channel through which agents keep improving and a documented source of harm, and this paper is the first clean measurement of when it's one or the other.

Since most textbook quantum speedups are low-depth and parallel (Grover-style), this shifts the burden of proving broad advantage onto structured problems, and it carries new implications for BPP vs BQP relative to a random oracle. A result you will see cited as the reference for "where quantum advantage must live" going forward.

**Realizing Logical Diagonal Gates via Transversal Physical Z-Rotations in CSS Codes**
K. Sai Mineesh Reddy, Navin Kashyap — [arXiv:2608.19094](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19094)
Fault-tolerant gate sets remain the bottleneck for CSS-code-based machines, and most constructions pick up magic-state overhead to go beyond Clifford. This paper gives a systematic "appending construction": take any CSS code and add a computed block of physical qubits on which you can apply a plain *transversal* Z-rotation to realize a chosen logical diagonal gate (single- or multi-controlled), while keeping the logical dimension fixed. That is essentially free fault tolerance for a useful family of logical gates, versus magic-state distillation. It is an architectural result — the kind of thing that quietly changes overhead estimates for code stacks that assume you need full magic state factories for everything.

**Quantum circuit optimization using deep reinforcement learning: Applications across multiple gate sets**
Khoa Dang Tao, Sumin Jin, Muhammad Raza, Changhyoup Lee — [arXiv:2608.19103](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19103)
A clean, pragmatic take on RL for circuit compilation: instead of letting the agent rediscover commutations and trivial cancellations, they embed the deterministic Commutation-and-Reduction (CR) pass directly into the environment so the RL policy spends its capacity only on nontrivial optimizations. The result is transfer — an agent trained on smaller circuits removes ~2× more gates on 20-qubit Clifford+T circuits than a standard RL agent. Sits squarely at the useful intersection of quantum hardware and ML, and it's a concrete pattern (wrap deterministic passes around the stochastic policy) that generalizes beyond this specific compilation problem.

---

## 2. Machine learning

**Learned, Then Lost: A Measured Single-Example Counterfactual in Pre-training**
Zachary Speck, Asa Shepard — [arXiv:2608.19168](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19168)
Ran the experiment nobody has done at scale: trained 32 small GPT-2 models from scratch on OpenWebText, injecting a single fixed passage (or a fabricated-subject twin, or random noise) into one batch row at peak learning rate, and compared each finished model to its uninjected twin. The finding is a clean measured decay — every geometric measure (loss barrier, CKA, weight displacement) shows the passage was learned within dozens of steps and then *fully* decayed by the end, with the model remaining in the same basin. Most of what we believe about how long single examples persist in LLMs is speculation; this is a direct measurement, even if it's at 124M parameters, and it's directly relevant to every "memorization / data-provenance" argument in the field.

**Beyond Teacher Likelihood: Group-Calibrated On-Policy Distillation for Long-Context Reasoning (GC-OPD)**
Zhu Zhang, Jixun Wang, et al. — [arXiv:2608.19181](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19181)
Identifies a specific and previously underdiagnosed failure mode in on-policy distillation (OPD): the teacher's token-level preference distribution is progressively *wronger* on long-context tasks as context grows, relative to a task-competent verifier, because the teacher itself loses track of distributed evidence. Their fix (GC-OPD) computes a signed "teacher vs verifier disagreement residual" per rollout group and uses relative-advantage credit assignment to decide where the verifier should override the teacher signal, preserving dense OPD where it's informative. Gets a substantial jump over vanilla OPD on five long-context benchmarks. This is a useful diagnostic pattern — *when should you trust the verifier over the teacher?* — that generalizes well past their specific setup.

## 3. Recursive self-improvement

**SPADE: Self-Play in Adaptive Synthetic Executable Environments**
Bo Liu, Simon Yu, Yiding Jiang, Ao Qu, et al. (incl. Zhaorun Chen, Yejin Choi, Natasha Jaques) — [arXiv:2608.19197](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19197)
The cleanest expression of the "self-improvement requires ever-growing goal distribution" thesis in this batch. One LLM plays two roles: an Environment Designer that writes stateful, multi-turn executable RL environments (Gym-style reset/step with reward + verification) and a Reasoning Agent trained in them. The key design decision is the *regret signal* — the agent's performance gap with vs. without privileged hints — which the Environment Designer optimizes by generating tasks right at the agent's capability frontier. The +5.3 average and +13.9 on agent tool-use benchmarks over the strongest fixed-environment baseline at 30B scale shows this is a concrete, working result, not a concept paper. This is the design pattern (regret-optimized environment curator) I'd want to keep on my radar for the next year of "agents improve from their own play" research.

**Eureka: Task-Conditioned Meta-Agent Orchestration for Scientific Discovery**
Alizer Wong, Heng Cui, Yi Tan, et al. — [arXiv:2608.19047](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19047)
Ambitious: a Meta-Agent that compiles long-horizon tasks into explicit "obligation graphs" with acceptance semantics, forms specialized Macro-Agents (state, memory, verifiers, topology) via receding-horizon planning and *architecture promotion*, and evolves the local architecture when bottlenecks recur. {"url": "https://inherentlabs.ai/research/training-to-replicate", "content_type": "text/html; charset=utf-8", "truncated": false, "text": "inherent
Research

Training AI Scientists to Replicate Research
14
th
August 2026
Read the paper
↗
In 1821, Richard Phillips asked his friend Michael Faraday to write a review of the emerging field of electromagnetism. Faraday was a strange choice for the task. The British scientist had little formal education and limited experience in the field. But he was a well-known experimentalist.
To write his review, Faraday decided to replicate past results manually. In the course of his experiments from the candlelit basement of the Royal Institution, Faraday found he could make a wire carrying current move around a magnet. “Very satisfactory”, he wrote in his journal. Faraday had invented the electric motor.
Inspired by Michael, we introduce
Faraday
, a 27B-parameter “AI Scientist” agent that outperforms Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 on the task of replicating research. Trained via long-horizon RL with coding agents as a tool, Faraday learns the skills of a rigorous scientist, a step towards AI Scientists capable of innovation across domains.
Faraday outperforms Claude Opus 4.8 (“Claude”) and GPT-5.5 (“Codex”) on paper replication tasks.
From replication to innovation
To train Faraday, we introduce
Replica
, a scalable space of RL tasks. Each task requires an agent to replicate a figure from a research paper with a limited time and compute budget, and without access to the original plot. The initial suite comprises 310 tasks from 100 ML and AI-for-science papers, in domains as diverse as natural language processing, materials science and weather forecasting.
We run recent agents from the leading labs on Replica and find that they do not saturate the task space. For Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 baselines, we run the model in the Claude Code and Codex harnesses respectively, with thinking effort set to extra high. Faraday produces more faithful replications for every category of paper in the task suite, and struggles less with recent research, effectively applying its scientific skills to work unseen by the base model at pre-training.
Faraday replicates more effectively than baseline agents across domains, with a particularly pronounced advantage in meta-learning, structural biology and materials science.
Replicating a figure may not seem like an especially innovative task. But looking at the process, rather than the output, replication becomes a stepping stone towards innovation. Research papers describe what the authors found that worked, not the negative results that got them there. To succeed, agents must recover the “99% perspiration” that does not appear on the page. This requires the hypothesis-driven exploration characteristic of open-ended research.
Replication forms the basis for a curriculum of underspecified tasks. Features beyond single plots can be removed from papers given to agents to replicate. Resource constraints can be further tightened or relaxed. Papers can even be imagined, leading the same Faraday model to innovate without knowing it.
RL for non-verifiable domains
Perfectly reproducing a plot is not the same as a successful replication, which also requires strong experimental design, good scientific practice, faithfulness to the claims of the original paper, and effective use of available resources. Ultimately, replication requires “research taste”.
We design an LLM judge and run a human study to validate that it captures the research taste of experts. But training on LLM judges remains challenging, because the stochasticity of the underlying model creates a noisy reward signal. We use per-task rubrics to solve this problem, achieving greater consistency and lower noise than an LLM baseline.
Our auto-generated rubric judge is more consistent and agrees more with humans.
To address the instability typical of long-horizon RL training, we make two further train-time modifications to our judge: multi-sample aggregation and turn-level credit assignment. Trained using this recipe, Faraday learns to become a more rigorous scientist.
Scalable scientific oversight
Faraday employs GPT-5.5 Codex as a tool, much like human scientists use coding agents. Remarkably, Faraday directs the work of a model several orders of magnitude larger in a way that improves replication performance.
Moreover, Faraday can generalise to directing a more capable agent at test-time, adapting to GPT-5.5 Codex after training with GPT-5.4-mini. As frontier coding agents continue to advance, we expect that the value of scientific judgement will only increase.
Faraday builds on previous discoveries to find new insights at test-time, similarly to existing AI Scientist agents. But unlike these agents, Faraday requires no hand-coded evolutionary harness, and has no test-time reward. In other words, Faraday learns to value discoveries intrinsically.
Faraday uncovers insights without the use of an evolutionary harness.
Future directions
Faraday represents the first step in a new paradigm that combines a layer of scientific intuition with the advancing capabilities of coding agents. We believe that better AI Scientists, powered by novel infrastructure and new forms of human-machine teaming, can benefit all of society.
At Inherent, Faraday’s improvements compound through the entire company, enabling us to discover new knowledge while firmly keeping humans in the loop. With an eye to safety, we are investigating how our methods might advance scalable oversight and ameliorate reward hacking.
We are building a new kind of AI and a new kind of research institution, fit for the age of AI-driven scientific discovery. To join us on our mission,

# Research Paper Digest — 2026-08-16

*Run: nightly scheduled digest. Sources: arXiv API (quant-ph / cs.LG feeds) plus cross-category keyword queries. The arXiv API in this environment's date filter was broken, so the digests come from the newest-indexed submission batches (the latest daily listings, submitted 2026-08-12 to 2026-08-13). ## 1. Quantum Computing

### Exponential quantum advantage for learning signals with a single qubit
**Authors:** Ishaan Kannan, Sridhar Prabhu, Saeed A. Khan, Mandar M. Sohoni, Xingrui Song, Saswata Roy, Alen Senanian, Valla Fatemi, Peter L. McMahon, Jordan Cotler
**Link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13521

The genuinely new thing is the QPsi (Quantum Phase-Space Inference) framework, which converts an experimental objective + constraints into both a tight lower bound on classical performance *and* the optimal quantum-enhanced algorithm, plus a certifiable quantum advantage. That's a much bigger deal than the experimental demo (which shows a 10^7 fold reduction on Fourier-learning with a single superconducting qubit), because it gives a systematic method for finding *where* quantum sensing helps, outside the quantum Fisher information regime where most previous claims live. If the lower bounds are right, "a qubit helps classically-sensing" moves from hand-waved to a design principle. Watch the QPsi lower-bound assumptions carefully — that's where the claims will be stress-tested.

### Universal magic state concentration
**Authors:** Jacopo Rizzo, Lorenzo Leone
**Link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13376

Existing magic-state distillation assumes the inputs are *some known* noisy state near a target; this is the first protocol that takes a **few copies of an unknown pure non-stabilizer qubit state** and outputs an **exact** target magic state via a fixed stabilizer circuit. The six-copy CCZ concentration result (necessary and sufficient, with the optimal success probability set by a stabilizer Renyi entropy M^lin_3) is new and I don't think the tightness is well-established elsewhere. This matters for fault-tolerant architectures that generate magic states on-the-fly from state-preparation hardware — if your source is only "a qubit in some non-stabilizer state," you can still get exact magic, which loosens a real practical constraint on hardware error rates.

### Quantum simulation of non-Markovian dynamical systems
**Authors:** Abtin Ameri, Arkopal Dutt, Hari Krovi
**Link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13533

Most quantum simulation literature covers Markovian dynamics, where the future depends only on the present state. This paper attacks the class of Volterra integro-differential equations with memory kernels and shows exponential speedups over classical ODE simulation *for the general-kernel case where M<1*, plus lower bounds showing the problem becomes intractable when M>=1 (so the quantum speedup is genuinely structural, not an artifact of a favorable regime). The "Markovianization" move — converting VIDEs with structured kernels into ODEs and then using standard techniques — is a clean trick that should transfer to other physics. Worth watching if you care about open quantum systems or fluid dynamics on a quantum processor in 3-5 years.

### Entanglement distribution and quantum storage of >8000 modes over a metropolitan network
**Authors:** Angelo Gelmini Rodriguez, Louis Nicolas, Theo Sanchez Mejia, Pavel Sekatski, Nicolas Brunner, Towsif Taher, Rob Thew, Philippe Goldner, Mikael Afzelius
**Link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13177

The real number here isn't "quantum repeater node" (those have been demo'd before), it's the **8235 temporal modes stored for 63 microseconds in a live Geneva municipal fiber network**, with a 979nm photon entangled to a telecom photon propagating 25.3km. The rare-earth ion ensemble memory is doing something genuinely new: multimode storage at 250MHz bandwidth with 76.6us lifetime, validated with a quantitative mode-capacity metric. If this scales, quantum repeater networks stop being bottlenecked on entanglement generation rates and start bottlenecking on network topology, which is a fundamentally different engineering problem.

### Classical simulation and design frontiers for IBM's doped Clifford sampling experiment
**Authors:** (not fully captured in API response — see arXiv)
**Link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13110

Classically simulates a 70-qubit, 70-layer IBM doped-CNOT random circuit (468 T-gates) using a temporal-boundary tensor network contraction. The claim is that their width is *provably minimal* (Ratcatcher-certified) for the tested instances, so they're not being beaten — the architecture of the circuit is such that the tensor-network width is fundamentally large. The paper's real value is the empirical data point: a real hardware-produced output distribution, 2051 amplitudes, 37.3 minutes on 256 H100 GPUs, 256GiB largest tensor per batch. If the XEB estimate (0.35034) is compatible with IBM's fidelity claim, the "quantum advantage" for this specific experiment is *much narrower* than the popular framing implies.

## 2. Machine Learning

### Vero: Can AI agents build formally verified software repositories?
**Authors:** Zhe Ye, Hantao Lou, Yuechun Sun, Peiyang Song, Zhengxu Yan, Timothe Kasriel, Qingyang Zhang, Kaiyu Yang, Soonho Kong, Jingxuan He, Dawn Song
**Link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13522

First benchmark to evaluate *joint* code+proof synthesis across **whole multi-module repository instances** (43 instances, Lean 4, spanning crypto protocols, distributed systems). The key design decision that makes this useful rather than another function-level coding benchmark is the **audit mechanism**: agents can prove the spec is unsatisfiable or the reference implementation is wrong, which surfaces hidden bugs in the curated data. That self-audit loop is what makes the benchmark credible. The finding that frontier agents solve only 27/43 and close zero on the hardest repos is a meaningful negative result — verified-code generation is not an incremental extension of current coding-agent capability.

### DARTree: Speculative diffusion decoding with autoregressive draft trees
**Authors:** Tianyi Li, Yaxin Luo, Xinyi Shang, Zhiqiang Shen
**Link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13524

Speculative decoding for LLMs (accept multiple draft tokens in one verification step) is well-studied; this extends it to **diffusion-based drafters** (which predict whole token blocks in parallel) and adds an AR-correction tree over the diffusion output. The 98.6% improvement in accepted-length over DFlash, 9.73× speedup, is a real inference-cost win for diffusion LLMs. What's genuinely new: a clean separation between drafting (diffusion, fast) and verification (AR tree, lossless), and decoupling the AR-head inference from heap operations so it's batchable. If you're serving diffusion-based LLMs at scale, this is the kind of paper that changes your cost model.

### Defensive Boosting for Online Probabilistic Forecasting
**Authors:** Georgy Noarov, Aaron Roth
**Link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13554

Online boosting has two existing guarantees that are *incomparable*: gradient boosting is competitive with the best span of H on all sequences, weak-to-strong boosting drives error to zero under a weak-learning condition. This paper gives a single algorithm that satisfies **both simultaneously** on every adaptive stream, and does it with just one weak-class learner (the previous methods maintain large ensembles). The ex-post hard-core certificate is a neat mechanistic insight: if the weak-learning condition is violated, the mistake weights *are* the certificate. It's a clean theoretical result from two people who both do serious online-learning theory (Noarov has published extensively here, Roth does theory+robustness). Worth a read if online probabilistic forecasting is in your stack.

### Synthetic Persona Pretraining: Alignment from Token Zero
**Authors:** Julian Minder, Viktor Moskvoretskii, Raghav Singhal, Difan Jiao, Andy Arditi, et al.
**Link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13482

Most alignment is applied post-pretraining, which means the persona is a thin overlay over whatever the pretraining data baked in. SPP annotates pretraining documents with value-aligned first-person reflections and pretrains on them, then does "persona binding" via instruction-tuning to tie the persona to the assistant identity. The key empirical finding is the **dose-timing result**: SPP applied early gives stronger constitution-following and better jailbreak robustness than the same intervention applied late; the gap grows with pretraining budget. That's a non-obvious, actionable result — *when* you do the intervention matters, not just *what* you do.

### LittleLearner: Language Models Under Pedagogically Controlled Knowledge Exposure
**Authors:** Fanfei Li, Jana Zeller, Manuel Prada-Corral, Thaddäus Wiedemer, Prasanna Mayilvahanan, Ryan Cotterell, Wieland Brendel
**Link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13545

Trains a 5B LLM on a 88B-token corpus *explicitly limited to US elementary-school material* (concepts, facts, vocabulary above Grade 5 excluded). The result is a model with functional language skills but with **knowledge and capability boundaries that map to interpretable curriculum guidelines**. That's a genuinely useful experimental tool: instead of "did the model know this because of pretraining data X?", you can ask "did it know this because we gave it this?" — which is a much cleaner ablation for knowledge-injection studies. Not a headline paper, but the kind of contribution that changes how people design alignment/education experiments.

## 3. Recursive Self-Improvement

### AutoDesign: Meta-Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Agentic Design
**Authors:** Yaxin Luo, Haobin Jiang, Jialv Zou, Xu Huang, et al. (14 authors)
**Link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13560

A meta-harness optimizer that takes rollout feedback from an agent's runs and *recursively improves the agent's harness* (the scaffolding around the model: prompts, tool-orchestration, workflows). Key distinction from "just fine-tuning the model": the harness is the mutable artifact, which is far cheaper and far more deployable than weight updates. The 253-tool-call, 11-edit-turn, $3 budget for a full autonomous loop reaching human conference-poster quality is a concrete, low-cost instance of the recursive-improvement pattern. The honest result: consistent gains (+12.4% average PosterBench score) across different code-agent backbones, which means the improvement is in the harness, not in any particular LLM.

### Practice Makes Unsafe: Skill Mis-evolution in Self-Improving LLM Agents
**Authors:** Xutao Mao, Liangjie Zhao, Xiang Zheng, Cong Wang
**Link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12851

This is the **safety paper in the room**. Self-improving agents convert successful trajectories into persistent cross-task skills. The problem: if a *malicious* trajectory happens to succeed, that skill gets distilled into the agent's persistent state and *survives after the malicious input is gone*. Their SkillMisevo-Bench measures this lifecycle explicitly (authoring → retrieval → later execution), and the finding is that all 21 evolved configurations author unsafe artifacts, 15 of which cause fresh-session harm. The SafeEvolve wrapper reduces unsafe retrieval by 26.7pp and fresh-session harm by 17.3pp, with 0.4pp utility loss. This is the first systematic treatment of the skill-mis-evolution problem, and it's a serious gap in current self-improvement systems. If you're building or deploying self-improving agents, this is the paper to read.

### AQuA: Recursively Self-Improving Quantitative Trading Research Agents
**Authors:** Jiacheng Guo, Suozhi Huang, Yunlong Gao, Zihao Li, Jian Ge, Xu Kuang, Mengdi Wang
**Link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12841

Two independent systems (one for factor discovery, one for trainable model development) each run their own closed loop: retain validated evidence from earlier experiments, use it to guide later proposals. The "recursive self-improvement" here is at the **research-process level**, not the model-weight level, which is a different (and arguably more realistic) framing. The results are concrete: IC ~0.190 on a crypto universe, +0.0843 per-stock IC on US equities, held-out Sharpe up to +2.50. The sealed sandbox (fixed data splits, fixed evaluator) is a good design choice — it means the improvements aren't just overfitting to the test set. This is a strong case that "research-loop" self-improvement is viable in a bounded, verifiable domain.

The quantum batch has real new results (magic-state concentration, non-Markovian simulation, the IBM simulation data point). ## 1. Quantum computing

### Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation with Adversarial Errors
**Nikolas P. Breuckmann, Louis Golowich, Umesh Vazirani** — https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16857

My take: this is the one paper in today's quantum batch I'd actually call a result, not an engineering advance. Prior FTQ theorems essentially assumed noise that is either local-and-stochastic or only corrupts a vanishingly small fraction of qubits per step. Here the adversary may flip an almost-linear number of physical qudits (`N^{1-o(1)}`) *every* timestep, i.e. a global, non-Markovian, worst-case noise model — and the depth overhead is only `\bar{N}^{o(1)}`, with poly-size overhead. The mechanism is a new subsystem product code family with local testability, plus recursive composition to drive the logical dimension to a constant. Two reasons this matters: (a) it directly neutralizes the "correlated noise kills logical qubits" objection that has held back the circuit-to-Hamiltonian route to quantum PCPs, and (b) Vazirani co-authoring a fault-tolerance result is a genre change, not incremental theory.

### Hundred-hertz quantum circuit iteration rate in a reusable neutral-atom array
**Liang Chen, Wen-Yi Zhu, Dong-Qi Ma, et al.** — https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16815

My take: neutral-atom machines have been winning on scale and coherence but losing on *throughput* — the "reconfigure the array" step is the bottleneck. This is a 10-qubit demonstration with non-destructive readout (99.7% retention) plus atom-reuse, hitting 101 Hz raw qCIR. Not a scaling breakthrough, but the framing is the point: they benchmark throughput the way classical chips benchmark MHz, and report a normalized Fisher-information-rate of 57.7 Hz as a hardware-level KPI. That's a useful primitive for whoever is deciding between neutral atoms and superconducting architectures for VQE/quantum-ML workloads specifically.

### Designing Quantum Error Correcting Codes to fit decoders via Reinforcement Learning
**Omer S. Sella, Robert Pinsler, Thomas Heinis** — https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15754

My take: the standard workflow is "here's a code family, please find a good decoder." This inverts it — fix the decoder architecture, and have PPO *generate* Bivariate Bicycle codes that make that specific decoder shine under depolarizing noise. Conceptually important because decoder quality and code structure are co-determined (same Pauli-frame information, different inductive biases), and this is a rare case where the *code* is treated as the learnable object rather than the decoder. It's a first cut on a small family (BB codes) and a single noise channel, so don't over-estimate — but the direction is worth tracking.

### Resolving and resetting the charge environment of single T-centers in silicon p-i-n waveguides
**Chaoshen Zhang, Hanbin Song, Lukasz Komza, et al.** — https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15993

My take: T-centers are one of the most promising telecom-band spin-photon sources on a *manufacturable* photonics platform, but their linewidth is dominated by charge noise. This demonstrates a physical reset — above-band illumination collapses the local charge ensemble — and reports the narrowest unheralded linewidth to date on an integrated T-center (128 MHz on the best of 46 emitters, 3.5× median improvement). Also reports coherent optical Rabi with 20 ns coherence. This is the kind of "boring hardware" result that actually unblocks scalable quantum networking rather than one more spin-squeezed photon source.

## 2. Machine learning

### Proteus: Incremental Memory Activation for Long-Context Sequence Modeling
**Reza Bayat, Ali Behrouz, Vahab Mirrokni, Aaron Courville** — https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16844

My take: this is a genuinely clean architectural observation. The whole line of memory-based long-context models (SWLA, Titans, Hope-Attention, Comba) shares an assumption: the memory state is *statically sized* across the sequence. The authors argue early tokens have no compression pressure and thus take up memory that later context needs; their fix is to *grow the effective capacity of memory as the context grows*, so early tokens are under an early bottleneck that forces compression, and late tokens see the newly-opened capacity. It's a zero-parameter mechanism that drops into existing memory backbones and reports wins that grow with context length. This is a design-principle paper in the best sense — "schedule capacity, not just tokens" — one I expect to appear in the next batch of long-context baselines.

### Le Critique: Privileged Value Functions for LLM Reinforcement Learning
**Siddarth Venkatraman, Matthieu Dinot, Laurence Aitchison** — https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16739

My take: GRPO's "sample a group of rollouts, take the mean" trick is now effectively the default for RL on LLMs, and the field has quietly decided critic-based RL is not worth the infrastructure. This is a direct challenge to that: (1) they design a *privileged* value function so the critic sees task-relevant signal that the policy doesn't — without injecting bias into the policy gradient — and (2) TETHER adaptively interpolates between group-relative and value-function baselines depending on how accurate the critic is, which is a clean answer to the classic "critic is worse than rollout means during training" failure mode. The claim "competitive with or better than mean-baseline GRPO" is what actually matters, because that's the bar every RL-on-LLM paper is implicitly held to.

### GEO-Flag: Detecting and Measuring GEO-Optimized Web Content
**Junjie Chu, Ye Leng, Mingjie Li, Yun Shen, Xinyue Shen, Yang Zhang** — https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16824

My take: GEO (Generative-Engine Optimization) is the emerging "SEO for LLM answers" field, and this is a detector *and* measurement instrument for it — 21 pages, 21 tables. Matters because if GEO-optimized content is now a non-trivial fraction of the web, every downstream LLM retrieval and RAG evaluation is biased, and we need to be able to *see* that. The methodological contribution (detection, not just a benchmark) is the differentiator versus one more "how LLMs rank results" paper.

## 3. Recursive self-improvement

### BaT: Towards Self-Evolving Medical Research Agent with Stage Rubrics
**Junqi Liu, Yufan He, Yexiao He, Pengfei Guo, Dong Yang, et al.** — https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16211

My take: this is the closest thing today to a *closed-loop* RSI paper with measurable numbers. BaT couples a Stage-Bank data pipeline that synthesizes curriculum outside the policy loop with BiCuRL (bilevel curriculum RL) — the outer level picks what to practice *next* via a fixed held-out evaluation, the inner level (policy update via GRPO) improves on that stage. The claim that a **9B agent beats Claude Opus 4.6 + Claude Code on AutoMedBench-Lite** (79.6 vs 77.5 overall) is the strongest empirical RSI number I've seen in this window, and it's on a domain where the agent's task is explicitly "medical-research" rather than toy puzzles. Also notable: they pre-register the ablation program and *report the failures at full prominence* rather than hiding them — for the field.

### JailbreakSkill: Scaling Automated Red-Teaming with Reusable and Ever-Evolving Skills
**Xiaoyu Wen, Jiajia Li, Zhida He, Peng Yu, Chenxu Wang, et al.** — https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16465

My take: this is a concrete instance of *recursive self-improvement with a closed loop*: an attack library, a diagnosis step, an evolution step (refine, combine, discover new skills), and an "add back to library" step. Reported gains are large — a 48.6-point macro-ASR lift against GPT-5.4 on AdvBench, plus emergent behaviors like "reframing a direct request as an unfinished document-completion task" that the agent produced *itself*, not a human prompt. Even if you're on the defensive side, that's the shape of threat the defender needs to plan for: not a fixed jailbreak set, but a skill library that grows from past attempts. This is one of the more consequential RSI papers of the last few days in the practical "security matters" sense of consequential.

### Competing at Every Price Point with Agentic Evolution over a Menu of LLMs (RoboPhD)
**Andrew Borthwick** — https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16207

My take: this inverts the framing. Instead of "train the next model," it treats a *menu of existing LLM endpoints* as the genome and a *meta-agent* (RoboPhD) as the evolutionary loop. Training pools are at most **100 examples**. It claims Pareto-domination of the frontier on DS-1000 (execution-checked code) and PaperFindingBench (scientific retrieval), including beating both the top-scoring and lowest-cost competing points. The significance is not the specific leaderboard positions (small tasks, single author) but the *mechanism*: agentic program evolution over a menu, driven by cost-constrained fitness, from small data. If the claim reproduces, the same skeleton applies anywhere "you can afford N LLM calls per answer" is the design constraint — which is most deployed agentic systems.

### Prior Audit-Repair Context Shifts LLM Verifier Thresholds Toward Leniency
**Parsa Mazaheri, Kasra Mazaheri** — https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16003

My take: small paper, important result. They measure that when the *same* LLM is wired as both checker and fixer (or two LLMs in a checker→fixer pipeline), the checker gets *more lenient*: 15-of-15 "model × wording" combinations show 2.8–11.5 pp fewer false alarms, with a *completed* audit→repair episode in context lowering false alarms even further. Signal-detection analysis localizes the shift to a movement in the threshold, not a change in discrimination. This matters directly for recursive self-improvement pipelines: if your verifier gets more forgiving because the *pipeline shape* tells it to, that's a systematic failure mode of the loop — not just a per-model property.

### Cross-topic observation
The RSI and ML lists overlap deliberately: BaT, RoboPhD, and JailbreakSkill all lean on RL + evaluation + curriculum machinery (BiCuRL/GRPO, value functions, skill libraries).
